projects.title: Production Planning Software
projects.tagline: Turns daily dealer requirements into machine and mould schedules.
projects.problem: Every morning planners had to turn the day's dealer orders into a factory schedule. That meant knowing which moulds were free, which machines they fit, which articles mattered most, and what was left over from yesterday. It was done by hand in Excel, so it was slow, decisions varied from person to person, and conflicts only showed up on the factory floor.
before: Orders consolidated by hand in Excel every morning.
Mould availability checked against a separate register.
Every order treated the same; no use of past sales.
Unfilled orders tracked informally.
after: One click builds the day's schedule from ERP data.
Mould–machine compatibility checked automatically.
Orders ranked by a priority score that uses past sales.
Unfilled demand carried forward to a visible backlog.
projects.solution: A Flask app with three layers kept apart, so heavy processing never slows the web pages: (1) data ingestion from the ERP, (2) a scheduling engine, (3) the planner interface. At its core, scheduling is a constraint problem: fit N requirements onto M moulds and K machines while respecting compatibility and capacity.
tech: Validation before scheduling: null checks on key fields, duplicate lines removed, unusually large quantities (above 3σ) flagged for review, invalid mould–article pairs rejected with a reason.
Priority score per dealer × article: dealer tier, 12-month sales velocity for the article in that region, days in backlog, and stock urgency.
Allocation: a weighted priority queue walks requirements in score order and assigns a compatible mould and machine until shift capacity runs out.
Compatibility matrix and machine capacity live in database tables that admins edit from the app.
Packaged with Docker so it deploys the same way on any server.
testing: Validation rules run on every load and report rejected rows instead of silently dropping them.
Every allocation and backlog decision is stored, so a planner can see why an order was not scheduled.
outcomes: The morning schedule is generated by the app instead of being built by hand.
Rules are applied the same way every day, and the backlog is visible instead of informal.

projects.title: Sales & Inventory Reporting System
projects.tagline: Daily ETL from ERP data into region-wise reports on a secure web portal.
projects.problem: Stock and sales reports (new launches, depot stock, leftover stock, category mix, plan vs. actual) were built by hand from ERP extracts and spreadsheets, then emailed around as files. Each region needed its own cut, and there was no single place to see the latest numbers.
before: Reports rebuilt by hand from extracts each day.
Files emailed region by region.
Nobody could tell whether a report was up to date.
Access controlled only by who got the email.
after: Scheduled scripts build every report table.
Users log in and see their own regions.
Status email after each ETL run.
Excel download, with product images, on demand.
projects.solution: Split into two parts: a set of Python ETL scripts that turn raw extracts and Excel masters into clean report tables, and a Flask portal that serves those tables with filters, role-based access and Excel export.
tech: One ETL script per report, so a failure in one does not block the others.
Region-mapping table decides what each user can see; filtering happens on the server, not in the browser.
Roles (admin / user), session timeouts and logging on every request.
Admins upload finance-related files that feed into the reports.
Excel export built with openpyxl, with product images embedded in the cells.
Caching on heavy report queries so repeat views load quickly.
Experiment: a chat endpoint that sends KPI summaries to a hosted open-weights LLM so users can ask questions in plain English.
testing: Each ETL run sends a status email, so a failed or empty load is noticed the same morning.
Request logging makes it possible to trace what a user saw and when.
outcomes: Reports are produced by scheduled scripts instead of by hand.
Each user pulls their own region's view whenever they need it.

projects.title: Retail Chain Sales & Stock Planner
projects.tagline: Combines retail partner files and plans stock with ABC classes and trend rules.
projects.problem: Sales, purchase-order and stock data from retail chain partners arrived as separate files in different formats. Comparing sales with targets and deciding how much to send meant merging these files by hand each time.
before: Partner files merged by hand.
Sales vs. target worked out in spreadsheets.
Replenishment based on gut feel and simple averages.
Order files typed up manually.
after: Daily ETL loads all partner files into one database.
Dashboards by store, article, category and state.
Rule-based planner suggests quantities per article.
Order files generated with product thumbnails.
projects.solution: A Flask platform built with blueprints (one per module: dashboards, PO mapping, master data, planning) on top of a MySQL database that the ETL jobs keep up to date.
tech: ETL normalises each partner's file layout into one schema before loading.
Purchase-order mapper links partner article codes to internal codes.
Demand planner: weighted-average sales, trend class (rising / flat / falling), ABC class by contribution, stock cover in weeks, and stock already in the pipeline.
Planner multipliers can be edited in the app, so the business can tune the rules without code changes.
Excel outputs with heat-map formatting (XlsxWriter) for quick reading.
Login, registration and password reset by email.
testing: PO mapping shows unmatched partner codes so they can be fixed before reports are trusted.
Planner suggestions can be checked against the stock cover and trend columns shown next to them.
outcomes: Sales against target and replenishment are planned in one place.
Order files that were typed by hand are generated automatically.

projects.title: Purchase-Order Demand Forecasting (ML research)
projects.tagline: Gradient-boosting ensemble that predicts next month's order quantity per article.
projects.problem: The rules-based planner uses weighted averages, which react slowly to trends and seasonality. The question was whether a machine-learning model could predict next month's purchase-order quantity per article more accurately.
before: Quantities planned from weighted averages.
Slow to react to a trend or a seasonal peak.
after: A model that learns from 60+ engineered features.
Measured on a held-out month before anyone relies on it.
projects.solution: Framed as supervised regression: each row is an article-month, the target is next month's PO quantity, and the features describe that article's recent history.
tech: Features: lags of past quantities, plus rolling mean, std, min and max over several windows (60+ in total), and an encoded category.
Models compared: XGBoost, LightGBM, scikit-learn gradient boosting and random forest.
Final prediction is an ensemble of the strongest models, which smooths out individual model errors.
Time-aware split: the most recent month is held out completely and used only for the final check.
testing: 5-fold cross-validation on MAE to choose and tune models.
Final check on the held-out month with MAE, RMSE, R² and MAPE.
Compared against the existing average-based planner on the same month.
outcomes: A working forecasting pipeline that runs offline as a notebook and script.
Not yet connected to the planning app; next step is a longer back-test over several months before switching.

projects.title: Product Image Search Bot
projects.tagline: Chat-style search for product images, kept current by a nightly incremental sync.
projects.problem: Sales teams constantly needed product images for specific articles and colours. The image library was large, lived in cloud storage, changed often, and had no search, so people asked colleagues or browsed folders.
before: Images found by browsing folders or asking someone.
No way to know if an image had been replaced.
No record of which images people couldn't find.
after: Search by article, colour or category, or upload a list.
Nightly sync downloads only new or replaced images.
Admin page shows top searches and missing images.
projects.solution: Two parts: a nightly ETL that keeps a local, indexed copy of the image library in sync with cloud storage, and a Flask chat-style app on top of it.
tech: Change detection: compares each object's ETag (content hash) with the last run to label it new, replaced or unchanged, so only changes are downloaded.
Regex-based parsing turns raw image file names into standard article + colour keys using a colour-code map.
Search with type-ahead suggestions; results downloadable as images, Excel or ZIP.
Security: OTP email login, self-registration with admin approval, HMAC-signed single-sign-on tokens from sibling apps, secrets encrypted with Fernet, hashed passwords.
Jobs scheduled with APScheduler; rotating log files.
testing: Every sync writes an exception report (unmatched names) and a replaced-images report.
Not-found search analytics show which articles still have no image.
outcomes: Any product image can be found from one search box.
Nightly sync avoids re-downloading the whole library.
Missing images are found from real search demand, not guesswork.

projects.title: Stock Catalogue Generator
projects.tagline: Upload a stock list and get a picture catalogue with MRP as PDF, Excel or ZIP.
projects.problem: To share available stock with dealers, someone had to look up each article's image and MRP by hand and paste them into a document.
before: Images and prices looked up one article at a time.
Catalogues assembled by hand.
Missing images found only when someone noticed.
after: One upload produces the whole catalogue.
PDF, Excel-with-images or ZIP output.
Daily email lists articles without images.
projects.solution: A Flask app that joins the uploaded stock list with a cached product master and MRP table, finds and stamps each image, and renders the chosen output format.
tech: Product master cached in memory, so joins don't hit the source every time.
Images stamped with the article code using Pillow.
PDF catalogues laid out with ReportLab; Excel files with embedded images via XlsxWriter.
Separate parallel downloader (ThreadPoolExecutor) pulls images from cloud storage with retries and can resume after a failure.
User management and activity logging in SQLite; scheduled jobs with the schedule library.
testing: Unmatched articles are listed in the output instead of being skipped silently.
Scheduled missing-image email acts as a daily data-quality check.
outcomes: A catalogue that needed manual lookups is produced from one upload.
Image gaps are reported every day instead of being found late.

projects.title: Power BI Sales Portal
projects.tagline: One portal that shows each user only the Power BI reports they're allowed to see.
projects.problem: Different people needed different slices of the same Power BI reports. Giving everyone workspace access was expensive and too broad, and sharing screenshots went out of date.
before: Reports shared as screenshots or exports.
Access was all-or-nothing at workspace level.
after: One portal; each user sees only their reports and pages.
Admins manage access without touching Power BI.
projects.solution: A Flask app that authenticates with Azure AD on the server and uses the Power BI REST API to generate embed settings for each user, according to rules kept in its own database.
tech: Server-side service authentication with MSAL; tokens never reach the browser beyond the embed token.
Admin screens register report sources, pages and filters, and map them to users.
DAX queries discover columns and distinct values to build filter menus, and pull data for Excel export.
User and activity tables in SQLite; automatic logout after inactivity.
testing: Access rules are checked on the server for every embed request.
Activity log shows who opened which report.
outcomes: Each user gets their own view inside one portal.
Access changes are made in the app in seconds.

projects.title: Product Launch Mailer
projects.tagline: Sends region-wise launch emails with product images from one spreadsheet.
projects.problem: For each product launch, announcement emails were put together region by region by hand. Missing or wrong images were often found only after the mail had gone out.
before: Emails assembled region by region.
Images attached by hand.
Missing images discovered after sending.
after: One upload builds every region's email.
Missing images flagged before sending.
History of every launch kept.
projects.solution: A Flask app that reads the launch sheet, joins it with the colour map and image library, checks for gaps, then renders and sends one HTML email per region.
tech: Images resized with Pillow and embedded in the email body.
HTML emails written with normal CSS, then inlined with premailer so they look right in every mail client.
Region-to-recipient mapping stored in SQLite and editable in the app.
Configuration and secrets loaded from a .env file.
Signed single-sign-on link hands the user over to the image search bot.
testing: Missing-image list can be downloaded and fixed before anything is sent.
Launch history log records what was sent, to whom and when.
outcomes: Launch mails go out the same way every time, with no broken images.

projects.title: Dealer Stock Allotment Engine
projects.tagline: Splits limited stock across dealer orders using a weighted scoring rule.
projects.problem: When dealer demand is higher than available stock, someone has to decide who gets what. This was done by hand in Excel, varied by person, and left no record of why a dealer got less.
before: Allotment decided by hand in Excel.
Different people applied different rules.
No record of why an order was cut.
after: One script run applies the same rules every day.
Every order line gets a clear Green / Red / Black status.
Every decision logged with its reason.
projects.solution: A pandas script that scores every dealer × article requirement, sorts by score, and allocates stock in that order until it runs out, then labels each line.
tech: Composite score as a weighted dot product (NumPy) of dealer priority, stock ratio, recent offtake, blocking flags and trend.
Allocation loop: highest score first; stock for each article is reduced as it is allotted.
Green = full quantity, Red = partial or deferred, Black = blocked (for example dues or no stock in the pipeline).
Excel output with row colours so the distribution team can read it at a glance.
testing: Input validation catches unknown dealer or article codes and empty quantities before scoring.
Audit table stores requested vs. allotted quantity and the reason for every line.
outcomes: Allotment follows the same transparent rules every day.
Any dealer query can be answered from the audit log.

projects.title: Crypto Price Range & Direction Research
projects.tagline: Can 1-second market data predict short-term moves after trading fees? A careful test.
projects.problem: Many trading backtests look profitable because of hidden data leakage or because they ignore fees. I wanted to find out honestly whether short-horizon price ranges and direction can be predicted well enough to make money after costs.
before: Common approach: one backtest, no leakage checks, fees ignored.
Good-looking results that don't hold up live.
after: Placebo and synthetic tests to catch leakage.
Walk-forward backtests with fees.
Results reported even when negative.
projects.solution: Treat it as two separate prediction problems: how far the price can move (volatility / range), and which way it will move (direction). Each model only gets used if it beats a simple baseline on data it has never seen.
architecture: Public exchange archive (1s spot, 1m futures) + live recording
tech: Volatility: ridge regression on realised variance over several windows, trading activity, jumps and time of day.
Ranges: quantiles of volatility-scaled returns, recalibrated on a rolling recent window.
Direction: strongly regularised logistic regression on order-flow imbalance, recent returns and the futures–spot gap; switched on only if it beats the base rate out of sample.
A small wide-and-deep neural network written in plain NumPy learns a correction on top of the linear model, with early stopping.
Horizons studied from 10 seconds to 20 minutes.
Local paper-trading dashboards and auto-written markdown reports; never places real orders.
testing: Placebo test: labels shuffled; any 'skill' found here means leakage.
Synthetic no-signal data: the pipeline must find nothing.
Walk-forward backtests including trading fees.
Unit tests on the pipeline.
outcomes: Range forecasts were well calibrated.
Direction was close to chance.
No strategy was profitable after fees, and that is reported plainly. The value is the evaluation method.
